summary: Discovery for private inference gateway for EmberGate, focus on VPC peering, private endpoints, KMS integration, and regional constraints. Customer leaning toward private Dedicated but evaluating latency/cost tradeoffs and zero-trust ingress. Next: share diagrams, schedule perf bench, and confirm regions.
transcript:
[00:00] Arielle Mendoza: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya here, Head of Platform at EmberGate. We'll mostly be focused on network and security.
[00:13] Tomás Rivera: Tomás, cloud architect, I own VPCs and peering.
[00:16] Hannah Li: Hannah, security, looking at KMS and audit requirements.
[00:19] Leo Park: Leo, dev, will run the integration work.
[00:22] Arielle Mendoza: Great, Marcus and Sasha from Redwood are with me - Marcus will cover the networking patterns, Sasha will cover security and runtime details.
[00:31] Marcus Lee: Hey all, thanks. High level — EmberGate is evaluating a private inference gateway model where your requests route from your VPC into a Redwood private dataplane via either VPC peering, transit gateway attachments, or private endpoints, correct?
[00:44] Tomás Rivera: Yep that's the idea. We need zero-trust ingress, and we want to avoid public internet egress for tokens or inference traffic.
[00:52] Marcus Lee: Totally. There are three common patterns we recommend: direct VPC peering (simple), Transit Gateway (recommended for multi-VPC or multi-region), and PrivateLink/private endpoint (when you need endpoint-specific security controls). Each has tradeoffs on routing and egress.
[01:08] Hannah Li: Quick question — do you support HSM-backed KMS integration for model encryption-in-use or just at-rest?
[01:14] Sasha Ivanov: Good Q. For Private deployments, customers can integrate their KMS/HSM for key wrapping and decryption at rest; we also support envelope encryption for model artifacts. We don't currently run customer HSMs inside our hosted control plane — for private customer-managed control planes you can bring your own HSM.
[01:30] Priya Shah: So for our compliance, we need CMK rotation and export controls, and we'd prefer no plaintext model parameters traversing Redwood-managed control channels.
[01:39] Sasha Ivanov: Understood. We can ensure model keys never leave your KMS for private deployments. We'll share the KMS integration doc that details key rotation and least-privilege IAM roles.
[01:49] Arielle Mendoza: Marcus, can you walk through port requirements and CIDR expectations?
[01:53] Marcus Lee: Sure. At a minimum, for VPC peering we need bi-directional TCP 443 for the control plane handshake and TLS token exchange. For inference traffic we prefer TLS on 443 as well. If you choose direct ICMP/metrics or remote debugging, there are a few additional ports but we usually keep those closed by default.
[02:10] Tomás Rivera: Does peering require overlapping CIDR restrictions? We use a handful of /16s, want to avoid renumbering.
[02:16] Marcus Lee: Peering cannot overlap, so if you have overlapping ranges we recommend Transit Gateway or AWS PrivateLink. Transit Gateway lets you NAT and do route mapping; PrivateLink avoids route overlap by exposing endpoint interfaces.
[02:28] Leo Park: PrivateLink sounds nicer for us from an ops pov, but worried about cross-region latency. We have users in eu-west-1 and us-west-2.
[02:37] Marcus Lee: PrivateLink is regional — endpoints are regional. For multi-region you'd deploy a regional private dataplane or use inter-region peering/transit. Redwood's Private product supports deploying control/data plane instances per region; we can replicate the model across two regions and replicate KV cache as needed. There's a cost implication.
[02:55] Tomás Rivera: What's the replication lag for KV cache — will it affect stateful chat sessions?
[03:00] Sasha Ivanov: KV replication is asynchronous across regions and we recommend session affinity to regional endpoints for low-latency chat. For failover, we do a best-effort warm start — not instant. If you need strict strong consistency across regions, we should scope that as a custom engineering effort.
[03:17] Hannah Li: On audit and logs — we need per-request audit logs forwarded to our SIEM, and at least 12 months retention. Can Redwood forward logs to our S3/Kinesis or do we pull them?
[03:28] Marcus Lee: For Private we have flexible log sinks — you can push to your S3 buckets (cross-account role), Kinesis or an on-prem collector over private link. We can also push structured traces to your OTLP endpoint. We'll add the exact schema.
[03:40] Priya Shah: Okay. Network egress: we want to ensure no egress to non-approved regions. How do you gate that?
[03:47] Marcus Lee: We implement region gating via route tables and our smart routing layer. For Private we can lock the dataplane to a set of allowed regions and reject request routings outside those. For Hosted, there are more constraints. We can also control model variants by region.
[03:59] Tomás Rivera: Any changes to our CIDR or route tables on our side for PrivateLink?
[04:04] Marcus Lee: For PrivateLink you'll create endpoint interfaces in subnets and allow specific security groups. No CIDR renumbering required. For peering you'd need unique subnets.
[04:14] Leo Park: How do we authenticate traffic? We want mutual TLS and tokens.
[04:18] Sasha Ivanov: We support mTLS for dataplane connections plus token-based auth managed by your SSO. For short-lived tokens we recommend integrating Redwood with your IdP for service-to-service SSO and issuing ephemeral keys.
[04:30] Hannah Li: Does Redwood support SAML or OIDC for service users?
[04:33] Arielle Mendoza: Yes, we support OIDC for machine identity via short-lived credentials; SAML for user SSO. We'll attach the integration guide.
[04:40] Tomás Rivera: Risk question — if we choose Dedicated vs Private, what's the isolation story?
[04:45] Marcus Lee: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools within Redwood-managed infrastructure with tenancy isolation and stronger SLOs. Private gives you a customer-managed control plane (VPC, VPC endpoints, your KMS) so you have full control over networking and key management. Dedicated is easier to run but Private gives you the strongest compliance posture.
[05:02] Priya Shah: Cost wise, Dedicated or Private — roughly how do they compare?
[05:05] Sasha Ivanov: Ballpark: Dedicated monthly reserved clusters are cheaper than full Private because you're still on Redwood infra; Private has higher fixed platform fees but gives you the isolation. We'll provide a cost model for your expected throughput—need token-per-second and concurrency numbers.
[05:18] Leo Park: On the latency numbers — can we get p50/p95 for 1k/5k/10k token requests in us-west-2?
[05:25] Marcus Lee: Yes, we can run a perf bench. For dedicated GPU pools p50 is typically 60–120ms depending on model size; p95 varies with batch sizes. Larger token lengths push p95 higher. We'll schedule a 10k token bench for your workload.
[05:38] Priya Shah: Regulatory — we have EU data residency for certain projects. If we spin up a private dataplane in eu-west-1, does Redwood handle data residency gating?
[05:46] Sasha Ivanov: Yes. Private deployment in the region ensures data, logs, and S3 buckets remain in region per config. We'll document retention and cross-region replication options.
[05:56] Tomás Rivera: Is there a maintenance window impact for upgrades and kernel patches?
[06:00] Marcus Lee: For Private you control the timing of upgrades; Redwood provides a recommended window and upgrade artifacts. For Dedicated/Hosted we do rolling upgrades and provide notification and can offer canary channels to test.
[06:12] Hannah Li: Anything about SC-2 or external pen tests?
[06:16] Sasha Ivanov: We publish our SOC 2 summary and can share pen test reports under NDA. For Private we can also run joint pen tests if needed.
[06:24] Arielle Mendoza: Quick align on timeline — what's your ideal procurement/PO timeline?
[06:28] Priya Shah: We want a pilot in Q4 and prod early Q1. Budget cycles close end of August.
[06:35] Arielle Mendoza: Great — we'll try to get docs and proposal before budget review.
[06:40] Marcus Lee: Recap of technical items and open questions: 1) Decide between PrivateLink (regional) vs Transit Gateway (multi-VPC) for initial pilot; 2) Confirm regions for pilot (you mentioned us-west-2 and eu-west-1); 3) We'll run perf bench; 4) KMS integration doc and SOC2 notes to be shared.
[06:58] Tomás Rivera: For the perf bench, we'll provide a synthetic prompt set and sample concurrency and token length distribution.
[07:05] Priya Shah: Also want to check failure modes — what happens if KV cache warms and regen? Need more detail in runbook.
[07:12] Sasha Ivanov: We'll include a runbook for cache warm, failover, and model fallback: e.g., if regional dataplane is down we fail to a cold instance with higher latency but preserve correctness.
[07:22] Leo Park: Anything else from everyone's side?
[07:25] Hannah Li: Please add a note about encryption in transit and at rest specifics to the security doc.
[07:29] Arielle Mendoza: Absolutely. Final next steps recap: Marcus to send VPC peering diagram and port list, Sasha to send KMS and SOC2 docs, Marcus+Tomás to schedule perf bench, Priya to confirm regions.
[07:43] Tomás Rivera: Sounds good. We'll aim to confirm regions by Thursday.
[07:46] Arielle Mendoza: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the shared links and action items.
[07:50] Priya Shah: Thanks all, bye.

Notes: Transcript contains normal filler and some ASR mis-words; references to shared assets above.
